title: Nursing Scenario: Prioritization and Patient Safety
prompt: You're a nurse starting your shift on a medical-surgical unit with four patients. At the same moment: Patient A puts on the call light saying they suddenly feel short of breath; Patient B needs their scheduled 9am antibiotic that's now 20 minutes late; Patient C is asking for help to the bathroom; and Patient D's family is at the desk upset and wants to speak with you about the discharge plan. Talk me through how you'd prioritize, what you'd do, and when you'd get help. This is educational — I'm assessing your reasoning, not medical advice.
blurb: An entry-level prioritization scenario — assessed for ABC-based triage, patient safety, appropriate escalation, and clear communication under competing demands.

rubric.label: Prioritization logic
rubric.description: Correctly ranks the competing demands using an appropriate framework (ABCs, Maslow, acute-vs-stable, actual-vs-potential problems), and can justify why the breathing patient comes first.

rubric.label: Patient safety
rubric.description: Keeps safety central: recognizes the shortness of breath as potentially urgent, doesn't leave an unstable patient, and addresses fall risk for the patient needing the bathroom rather than ignoring it.

rubric.label: Assessment approach
rubric.description: Describes a focused assessment of the urgent patient (look at the patient, vitals/SpO2, position upright, apply oxygen per protocol) rather than jumping to conclusions or interventions without assessing.

rubric.label: Escalation & help-seeking
rubric.description: Knows when and how to call for help — delegate appropriately to a CNA/colleague, escalate to charge nurse/rapid response/provider using a structured handoff (e.g. SBAR) if the patient deteriorates.

rubric.label: Delegation & teamwork
rubric.description: Delegates the lower-acuity tasks appropriately (assistive personnel for the bathroom, a colleague or charge nurse to hold the family, note the antibiotic timing window) rather than trying to do everything alone.

rubric.label: Communication
rubric.description: Communicates clearly and calmly with patients, family, and team; explains reasoning and manages expectations without dismissing anyone.

reference.scenario: Entry-level nursing prioritization scenario. This is educational and framework-based — it assesses clinical reasoning and safety judgment, not real medical direction. The candidate faces four simultaneous demands of different acuity and must prioritize, act, delegate, and escalate. The correct first priority is Patient A (sudden shortness of breath) because airway/breathing/circulation (ABCs) outrank everything else — sudden dyspnea is a potential airway/breathing emergency and an actual, not potential, problem. A strong entry-level answer goes to Patient A first, does a rapid focused assessment (look at the patient's work of breathing and color, check SpO2 and vitals, sit them upright, apply oxygen per unit protocol), and — critically — does not leave that patient if they appear unstable, instead calling for help. It uses the team: delegate the bathroom assist to a CNA/assistive personnel while noting Patient C's fall risk (don't just tell them to wait unsupervised if they're a fall risk), recognize the antibiotic (Patient B) has a timing window and is important but not immediately life-threatening — it can be given within the acceptable window once the emergency is handled, or delegated appropriately per scope — and ask the charge nurse or a colleague to acknowledge Patient D's family and set a time to talk, since an upset family is a communication priority but the lowest clinical acuity. If Patient A deteriorates, escalate promptly via rapid response / charge nurse / provider using a structured SBAR handoff. The best answers name their framework (ABCs, acute vs stable, actual vs potential), stay calm, and keep reassessing. Weak answers do tasks in the order presented, chase the loudest voice (the family) or the easy task first, leave an unstable patient, fail to delegate, never escalate, or intervene on the dyspneic patient without assessing.
model_points: Prioritize with a framework: ABCs first — Patient A's sudden shortness of breath is a breathing problem and an actual (not potential) problem, so it outranks the antibiotic, the bathroom, and the family. Say the framework out loud.

Go to Patient A first and do a rapid focused assessment: look at the patient (work of breathing, color, level of consciousness), check SpO2 and vital signs, sit them upright, and apply oxygen per unit protocol.
Do not leave an unstable patient: if Patient A looks unstable or worsens, stay and call for help rather than walking away to handle other tasks.

Delegate the low-acuity, non-clinical-judgment tasks: ask a CNA/assistive personnel to help Patient C to the bathroom — but flag fall risk so they aren't left unsafely; don't simply tell a fall-risk patient to wait alone.

Handle Patient B's antibiotic within its timing window: important and time-sensitive but not immediately life-threatening; give it once the emergency is controlled or delegate per scope, and document the timing.

Manage Patient D's family: acknowledge them and set expectations — ask the charge nurse or a colleague to greet them and schedule a moment to talk; an upset family is a real communication need but the lowest clinical acuity.

Escalate appropriately and early: if Patient A deteriorates, call the charge nurse / rapid response / provider, and hand off with a structured SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation).
Reassess continuously and communicate calmly with every patient and the family, explaining briefly why you're prioritizing and that you'll be back — no one should feel dismissed.
Work within scope and team: know what you can delegate versus what requires the nurse's own assessment and judgment.

probes.trigger: candidate does tasks in the order presented or picks the easy/loud one first
probes.question: Which patient do you see first, and why that one? What framework are you using to rank them?

probes.trigger: candidate goes to the breathing patient but jumps to interventions
probes.question: Before you do anything, what does your focused assessment of that patient look like — what are you checking?

probes.trigger: candidate leaves the unstable patient to do other tasks
probes.question: The patient still looks like they're struggling to breathe. Is it safe to leave them right now, and if not, what do you do instead?

probes.trigger: candidate tries to do everything alone
probes.question: You can't be in four places at once. Who on your team can help, and what would you hand off to them?
The patient who needs the bathroom is a fall risk. What's your responsibility there, and how do you keep them safe while you're with the other patient?
The breathing patient's oxygen level is dropping despite what you've done. Who do you call, and how do you communicate what's happening?
How do you keep the upset family from feeling ignored while you handle the emergency?

red_flags: Addresses patients in the order presented or handles the loudest/easiest first
Fails to recognize sudden shortness of breath as the top priority (ABCs)
Intervenes on the dyspneic patient without any assessment
Leaves an unstable patient unattended to do lower-acuity tasks
Never delegates or asks for help; tries to do everything alone
Never escalates even when the patient deteriorates, or escalates with no structured handoff
Dismisses the family entirely or lets them derail clinical priorities
follow_ups: Patient A's SpO2 is 86% on room air and not improving with what you've done. What now?
The CNA you wanted to delegate the bathroom to is on break. How does that change your plan?
How would you hand this off to the rapid response team in an SBAR format?
The family becomes more agitated and blocks the hallway. How do you handle it without abandoning your patient?
How late can that scheduled antibiotic be, and how do you decide when it becomes a problem?
reference.exemplar_answer: A strong entry-level answer leads with the framework: 'I'd prioritize by ABCs and acute-versus-stable. The sudden shortness of breath is a breathing problem and an actual emergency, so Patient A comes first — before the antibiotic, the bathroom, or the family.' Then assessment before intervention: 'I'd go straight to Patient A, look at their work of breathing, color, and alertness, check their oxygen saturation and vital signs, sit them upright, and apply oxygen per our protocol. I would not leave them if they look unstable — I'd hit the call light or ask a colleague to grab the charge nurse.' Using the team: 'While I'm assessing, I'd delegate — ask a CNA to help Patient C to the bathroom, but flag that they're a fall risk so they aren't left alone unsafely. The 9am antibiotic is important and time-sensitive but not immediately life-threatening, so it can be given within its window once the emergency is controlled, or handed to a colleague per scope. I'd ask the charge nurse to greet Patient D's family, let them know I'm handling an urgent situation, and set a specific time to sit down with them so they don't feel ignored.' Escalation: 'If Patient A's oxygen keeps dropping despite oxygen and repositioning, I'd call rapid response and the provider and hand off with SBAR — situation, background, assessment, and what I'm recommending.' Throughout, I'd stay calm, keep reassessing, and communicate briefly with each patient so no one feels dismissed. It ranks by acuity, assesses before acting, keeps the unstable patient safe, delegates, and escalates with structure.

interviewer_notes: This is an entry-level educational scenario — reward sound reasoning and safety instincts over encyclopedic clinical detail, and never coach real medical treatment. The single must-have is recognizing the sudden shortness of breath as the top priority via ABCs; if the candidate handles patients in presented order or chases the loudest demand (the family), probe for their prioritization framework. Then look for assess-before-intervene, not leaving an unstable patient, appropriate delegation (with fall-risk awareness for the bathroom patient), and knowing when/how to escalate with a structured SBAR handoff. Use the deterioration follow-up (SpO2 86%) to test escalation. Strong entry candidates name a framework, stay calm, delegate rather than martyring themselves, and keep every patient and the family feeling attended to. Penalize task-order-as-presented, intervening without assessing, abandoning an unstable patient, never asking for help, ignoring fall risk, and failing to escalate on deterioration.
